title: When One Channel Is Eighty Percent of Your Pipeline
content:
### **A Risk That Does Not Appear on Any Report** 

If one source produces most of your appointments, your business has a single point of failure. That is obvious stated plainly, and almost never accounted for, because the channel is working. 

###  **What Changes When It Falters** 

Crews and sales staff are fixed costs. When the primary channel softens, that cost does not move. There is no time to build a replacement, because building one takes months and the gap is immediate. 

So companies do the expensive thing: bid harder on the channel that is already declining, or buy shared leads at whatever the market asks. Both are decisions made from a weak position. 

###  **Why Diversifying Late Costs More** 

A second channel added while the first is healthy can start small, be measured honestly, and be scaled or stopped based on what it actually produces. 

A second channel added during a shortfall has to work immediately, gets judged on its first two weeks, and is usually abandoned before it has a fair chance. 

###  **A Reasonable Standard** 

No single source should be so large that its decline would be a crisis. For most companies that means at least two channels producing meaningfully, with a third being tested. 

That is not a marketing philosophy. It is the same logic any business applies to depending on a single supplier or a single large customer.
